claim: 15 native, right-handed German speakers (seven females, age range: 20–30 years) with no history of neurological disorders or cTBS contraindications participated in the study.
source: 15 native, right-handed German speakers (seven females, age range: 20–30 years) with no history of neurological disorders or cTBS contraindications participated in our study.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics and inclusion criteria in the Methods section.

claim: All subjects were included in the final analyses.
source: All subjects were included in the final analyses.
evidence: Direct statement about data inclusion in the Methods section.

claim: Phonological response speed was significantly longer than semantic response speed.
source: Overall, phonological response speed was significantly longer than semantic response speed (main effect of task: F1,14 = 13.69, p=0.002; η2= 0.56).
evidence: Statistical test results showing main effect of task on response speed.

claim: Phonological and semantic decisions were differentially affected by cTBS.
source: However, this effect significantly interacted with cTBS (AG vs. SMG vs. sham), indicating that phonological and semantic decisions were differentially affected by cTBS (F2,28 = 5.36, p=0.011; η2= 0.28; Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical interaction effect and reference to Figure 1C showing differential effects.

claim: cTBS over SMG significantly delayed phonological decisions when compared with sham cTBS.
source: Two-tailed post-hoc paired t-tests revealed that cTBS over SMG significantly delayed phonological decisions when compared with sham cTBS (t14 = 2.76, p=0.01; d = 0.73) or cTBS over AG (t14 = 3.20, p=0.006; d = 0.81).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical tests showing significant delay in phonological decisions after SMG cTBS.

claim: cTBS over SMG significantly delayed phonological decisions when compared with cTBS over AG.
source: Two-tailed post-hoc paired t-tests revealed that cTBS over SMG significantly delayed phonological decisions when compared with sham cTBS (t14 = 2.76, p=0.01; d = 0.73) or cTBS over AG (t14 = 3.20, p=0.006; d = 0.81).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical tests showing significant delay in phonological decisions after SMG cTBS compared to AG cTBS.

claim: There was a trend towards increased semantic response latencies after cTBS of AG relative to sham.
source: In contrast, for semantic decisions, there was a trend towards increased response latencies after cTBS of AG relative to sham (t14 = 2.15; p=0.05; d = 0.34) but not SMG cTBS (p=0.14; d = 0.13).
evidence: Statistical test showing trend-level effect on semantic response latencies.

claim: Task accuracy was not affected by cTBS.
source: Task accuracy was not affected by cTBS (all p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical results showing no significant effect on accuracy.

claim: cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity in left AG.
source: Relative to cTBS of neighbouring SMG, cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity not only at the stimulated area, but in a large network previously associated with semantic processing, including left AG (x,y,z = −42,–67, 28; T = 5.21); aIFG (x,y,z = −48, 41,–14; T = 6.64; x,y,z = −57, 26, 19; T = 6.48) and left posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG: x,y,z = −60,–43, −2; T = 5.55) (Figure 2A).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in AG with statistical values and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity in left aIFG.
source: Relative to cTBS of neighbouring SMG, cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity not only at the stimulated area, but in a large network previously associated with semantic processing, including left AG (x,y,z = −42,–67, 28; T = 5.21); aIFG (x,y,z = −48, 41,–14; T = 6.64; x,y,z = −57, 26, 19; T = 6.48) and left posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG: x,y,z = −60,–43, −2; T = 5.55) (Figure 2A).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in aIFG with statistical values and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity in left posterior middle temporal gyrus.
source: Relative to cTBS of neighbouring SMG, cTBS of AG significantly decreased task-related semantic activity not only at the stimulated area, but in a large network previously associated with semantic processing, including left AG (x,y,z = −42,–67, 28; T = 5.21); aIFG (x,y,z = −48, 41,–14; T = 6.64; x,y,z = −57, 26, 19; T = 6.48) and left posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG: x,y,z = −60,–43, −2; T = 5.55) (Figure 2A).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in pMTG with statistical values and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: There was no significant difference in task-related activity between cTBS of SMG and sham cTBS during semantic decisions.
source: There was no significant difference in task-related activity between cTBS of SMG and sham cTBS during semantic decisions.
evidence: Direct statement about lack of significant difference between conditions.

claim: cTBS over AG increased task-related neural activity in bilateral supramarginal gyrus during semantic decisions relative to cTBS over SMG.
source: Specifically, after cTBS over left AG vs. SMG, increased task-related neural activity was found in bilateral supramarginal gyrus (SMG, x,y,z = −45,–40, 46; T = 5.30; x,y,z = 42,,–44, 42; T = 5.00) and left posterior IFG/ventral premotor cortex (pIFG: x,y,z= −54, 5, 19; T = 5.28; Figure 2B).
evidence: fMRI results showing increased activity in bilateral SMG with statistical values and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: cTBS over AG increased task-related neural activity in left posterior IFG/ventral premotor cortex during semantic decisions relative to cTBS over SMG.
source: Specifically, after cTBS over left AG vs. SMG, increased task-related neural activity was found in bilateral supramarginal gyrus (SMG, x,y,z = −45,–40, 46; T = 5.30; x,y,z = 42,,–44, 42; T = 5.00) and left posterior IFG/ventral premotor cortex (pIFG: x,y,z= −54, 5, 19; T = 5.28; Figure 2B).
evidence: fMRI results showing increased activity in left pIFG with statistical values and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The individual suppression of task-related activity in AG after cTBS over AG relative to sham cTBS predicted the individual upregulation of semantic activity in SMG.
source: Notably, the individual suppression of task-related activity in AG after cTBS over AG relative to sham cTBS predicted the individual upregulation of semantic activity in SMG (regression, normalized to sham cTBS, R2 = 0.37, ß = −0.61, t = 2.79, p=0.016, two-tailed; Figure 3B).
evidence: Regression analysis showing predictive relationship between AG suppression and SMG upregulation.

claim: AG and aIFG are connected via the middle longitudinal fasciculus and extreme capsule.
source: Specifically, AG and aIFG were connected via a ventral pathway constituted by the middle longitudinal fasciculus and the extreme capsule (Saur et al., 2008), also termed as inferior fronto-occipital fascicle (Duffau et al., 2005) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Probabilistic fiber tracking results showing anatomical connectivity, with citations to previous work.

claim: cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in bilateral SMG/superior parietal cortex during phonological decisions.
source: Specifically, when contrasted with cTBS over AG or sham cTBS, cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in the bilateral SMG / superior parietal cortex, bilateral frontal operculum / pIFG and right supplementary motor area (Table 1).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in bilateral SMG/superior parietal cortex with reference to Table 1.

claim: cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in bilateral frontal operculum/pIFG during phonological decisions.
source: Specifically, when contrasted with cTBS over AG or sham cTBS, cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in the bilateral SMG / superior parietal cortex, bilateral frontal operculum / pIFG and right supplementary motor area (Table 1).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in bilateral frontal operculum/pIFG with reference to Table 1.

claim: cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in right supplementary motor area during phonological decisions.
source: Specifically, when contrasted with cTBS over AG or sham cTBS, cTBS over SMG decreased task-specific activity in the bilateral SMG / superior parietal cortex, bilateral frontal operculum / pIFG and right supplementary motor area (Table 1).
evidence: fMRI results showing decreased activity in right supplementary motor area with reference to Table 1.

claim: There was no upregulation of task-related activity during phonological processing after cTBS of SMG vs. cTBS of AG or sham cTBS.
source: We did not find any upregulation of task-related activity during phonological processing after cTBS of SMG vs. cTBS of AG or sham cTBS, even after reducing the threshold.
evidence: Direct statement about absence of upregulation even at reduced threshold.

claim: There were no significant differences in task-related activity between cTBS of AG and sham cTBS during phonological decisions.
source: There were no significant differences in task-related activity between cTBS of AG and sham cTBS during phonological decisions.
evidence: Direct statement about lack of significant differences between conditions.

claim: The winning DCM model had an exceedance probability of 79%.
source: Our winning model had an exceedance probability of 79%, while all other models had probabilities < 10%.
evidence: DCM model selection results showing exceedance probability.

claim: The winning DCM model identified modulation of the inhibitory connection from AG to aIFG as the best explanation for the data.
source: Among the 63 models tested (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), variational Bayesian model selection identified the model with driving input to SMG and modulation of the inhibitory connection from AG to aIFG as winning model.
evidence: DCM model selection results identifying the winning model with reference to figure.

claim: The intrinsic connection from AG to SMG was significantly different from zero.
source: These parameters included the intrinsic connection from AG to SMG (regardless of cTBS site, mean: 0.03, T = 3.27; p<0.006) and the modulation of the connection from AG to aIFG by cTBS of AG (mean: −0.19, T = 3.67 p<0.003).
evidence: DCM parameter estimates with statistical significance tests.

claim: The modulation of the connection from AG to aIFG by cTBS of AG was significantly different from zero.
source: These parameters included the intrinsic connection from AG to SMG (regardless of cTBS site, mean: 0.03, T = 3.27; p<0.006) and the modulation of the connection from AG to aIFG by cTBS of AG (mean: −0.19, T = 3.67 p<0.003).
evidence: DCM parameter estimates with statistical significance tests.

claim: The connection between AG and aIFG was more strongly modulated by cTBS of AG than SMG.
source: A direct comparison of the parameter estimates for cTBS of AG vs. SMG confirmed that the connection between AG and aIFG was stronger modulated by cTBS of AG than SMG (t14 = 2.92, p<0.026, paired t-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of DCM parameter estimates between conditions.

claim: The individual increase in the inhibitory drive from AG to aIFG after cTBS of AG predicted the individual delay in the mean semantic response speed after cTBS.
source: Importantly, the individual increase in the inhibitory drive from AG to aIFG after cTBS of AG predicted the individual delay in the mean semantic response speed after cTBS (regression, R2 = 0.62, ß = −0.79, t = 4.39, p=0.001, two-tailed; Figure 5B).
evidence: Regression analysis showing predictive relationship between connectivity and behavior.

claim: The individual upregulation of SMG after cTBS over AG was significantly correlated with the delay in semantic response speed after AG cTBS.
source: We found a significant correlation between the individual upregulation of SMG after cTBS over AG and the cTBS-induced delay in mean semantic response speed (normalized to sham cTBS, r = 0.54, p=0.036, two-tailed; Figure 5C).
evidence: Correlation analysis showing relationship between SMG upregulation and behavioral delay.

claim: Semantic decisions engaged bilateral AG and left aIFG at baseline (after sham cTBS).
source: Notably, we found increased task-related activity for (bilateral) AG and left aIFG during semantic decisions only, while phonological decisions increased task-specific activity in (bilateral) SMG and left pIFG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: fMRI results showing task-related activity patterns with reference to figure.

claim: Phonological decisions engaged bilateral SMG and left pIFG at baseline (after sham cTBS).
source: Notably, we found increased task-related activity for (bilateral) AG and left aIFG during semantic decisions only, while phonological decisions increased task-specific activity in (bilateral) SMG and left pIFG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: fMRI results showing task-related activity patterns with reference to figure.

claim: Previous studies associated semantic processing with increased neural activation of left-hemispheric temporal, inferior frontal and inferior parietal regions.
source: Previous studies associated semantic processing with increased neural activation of left-hemispheric temporal, inferior frontal and inferior parietal regions (Binder et al., 2009; Vigneau et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: Left angular gyrus and anterior inferior frontal gyrus were identified as semantic key nodes by means of focal perturbations induced with transcranial magnetic stimulation.
source: In particular, left angular gyrus (AG) and anterior inferior frontal gyrus (aIFG) were identified as semantic key nodes by means of focal perturbations induced with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) (Devlin et al., 2003; Sliwinska et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous TMS research findings with citations.

claim: Several TMS studies assigned the left aIFG a central role in semantic control processes.
source: Specifically, several TMS studies assigned the left aIFG a central role in semantic control processes (Hoffman et al., 2010; Whitney et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about previous TMS research findings with citations.

claim: The anterior temporal lobe is crucial for core semantic representations.
source: These regions include the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) for core semantic representations and the posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG) as another key node for semantic control aspects (Binney and Ralph, 2015; Davey et al., 2015; Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016; Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: The posterior middle temporal gyrus is a key node for semantic control aspects.
source: These regions include the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) for core semantic representations and the posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG) as another key node for semantic control aspects (Binney and Ralph, 2015; Davey et al., 2015; Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016; Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: The contribution of the left aIFG to semantic decisions crucially depends on the functional integrity of the left AG.
source: With respect to the interactions in the semantic network, it was shown that the contribution of the left aIFG to semantic decisions crucially depends on the functional integrity of the left AG (Hartwigsen et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: Left AG was able to compensate for a focal perturbation of aIFG during semantic decisions unless it was additionally perturbed with TMS.
source: Hence, left AG was able to compensate for a focal perturbation of aIFG during semantic decisions unless it was additionally perturbed with TMS, indicating a strong interaction between both regions.
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with implicit citation to Hartwigsen et al., 2016.

claim: TMS over neighbouring supramarginal gyrus selectively delayed phonological decisions but not semantic decisions.
source: In contrast, TMS over neighbouring supramarginal gyrus (SMG) selectively delayed phonological decisions (i.e., decisions on the sound of words) but not semantic decisions.
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with implicit citation to Hartwigsen et al., 2016.

claim: The AG showed increased task-related activity for words as compared to non-words or concrete relative to abstract words.
source: For instance, this region showed increased task-related activity for words as compared to non-words or concrete relative to abstract words (Binder et al., 2009; Seghier, 2013), but deactivation for other semantic tasks, with the amount of deactivation being correlated with increased task-difficulty (Humphreys et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: The AG showed deactivation for some semantic tasks, with the amount of deactivation being correlated with increased task-difficulty.
source: For instance, this region showed increased task-related activity for words as compared to non-words or concrete relative to abstract words (Binder et al., 2009; Seghier, 2013), but deactivation for other semantic tasks, with the amount of deactivation being correlated with increased task-difficulty (Humphreys et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: The AG contributes to functions outside the core language domain like episodic memory and social cognitive tasks.
source: Besides, the AG also contributes to other functions outside the core language domain like episodic memory and social cognitive tasks (Bzdok et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: The lasting cTBS-induced suppression of neuronal excitability should give rise to an acute adaptive reorganization within the non-affected functional nodes of the network to compensate for the cTBS-induced suppression of neuronal activity.
source: The lasting cTBS-induced suppression of neuronal excitability should give rise to an acute adaptive reorganization within the non-affected functional nodes of the network to compensate for the cTBS-induced suppression of neuronal activity (Siebner and Rothwell, 2003).
evidence: Statement about expected effects of cTBS with citation.

claim: Combined TMS-fMRI studies often reveal widespread stimulation effects, involving neighbouring and distant interconnected brain regions.
source: Indeed, combined TMS-fMRI studies often reveal widespread stimulation effects, involving neighbouring and distant interconnected brain regions (Bestmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: The upregulation of the neighbouring phonological network might have partially compensated for the disruptive effect on semantic decisions.
source: Moreover, semantic suppression induced upregulation in neighbouring phonological regions that might have partially compensated for the disruptive effect on semantic decisions.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting compensatory mechanism.

claim: The observed functional-anatomical double dissociation during semantic vs. phonological decisions supports the notion that both processes are subserved by different networks.
source: The observed functional-anatomical double dissociation during semantic vs. phonological decisions supports the notion that both processes are subserved by different networks (Hartwigsen et al., 2016) and suggests that these networks might differ in their potential to partially compensate for a focal disruption.
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation to previous work.

claim: The semantic and phonological networks might differ in their potential to partially compensate for a focal disruption.
source: The observed functional-anatomical double dissociation during semantic vs. phonological decisions supports the notion that both processes are subserved by different networks (Hartwigsen et al., 2016) and suggests that these networks might differ in their potential to partially compensate for a focal disruption.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting differential compensatory potential.

claim: A focal perturbation over a semantic key region can induce large-scale inhibitory effects on the network level.
source: These findings suggest that a focal perturbation over a semantic key region can induce large-scale inhibitory effects on the network level.
evidence: Interpretation of DCM results.

claim: The strong remote inhibition effects are behaviourally relevant.
source: These results show that the strong remote inhibition effects are behaviourally relevant.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation between connectivity and behavior.

claim: The remote inhibitory effects of AG cTBS in the semantic network were most probably mediated by long-distance cortico-cortical association tracts.
source: Constrained probabilistic fiber tracking of diffusion tensor imaging data further revealed that the strong remote inhibitory effects of AG cTBS in the semantic network were most probably mediated by long-distance cortico-cortical association tracts.
evidence: Interpretation of fiber tracking results.

claim: A topographically adjacent, yet functionally separate network may have the potential to partially support processing after disruption of a strategic key region in the language system.
source: We speculate that the relatively weak effect of AG cTBS on semantic decisions might be explained by the upregulation of the neighbouring phonological network that might have helped to maintain task processing. Indeed, the subject-specific degree of AG suppression after cTBS predicted the individual upregulation of neighbouring SMG. These results suggest that a topographically adjacent, yet functionally separate network may have the potential to partially support processing after disruption of a strategic key region in the language system.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting compensatory mechanism.

claim: A stronger individual disruption of the semantic network required a stronger contribution of the SMG to maintain task function.
source: We conclude that a stronger individual disruption of the semantic network required a stronger contribution of the SMG to maintain task function.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation between SMG upregulation and behavioral delay.

claim: Lower-level resources like phonological working memory capacities might be recruited to partially contribute to higher-level semantic tasks to preserve task processing, but not the other way round.
source: Specifically, the differential behavioural effects of cTBS over AG and SMG during semantic and phonological decisions suggest that lower-level resources like phonological working memory capacities (Nixon et al., 2004; Romero et al., 2006) might be recruited to partially contribute to higher-level semantic tasks to preserve task processing, but not the other way round.
evidence: Interpretation of results with citations to previous work on phonological working memory.

claim: AG perturbation might have increased the overall task demands, thereby necessitating the contribution of more general executive control regions.
source: As an equally plausible alternative explanation, AG perturbation might have increased the overall task demands, thereby necessitating the contribution of more general executive control regions.
evidence: Alternative interpretation of results.

claim: The upregulation of left SMG after cTBS of AG extended into the intraparietal sulcus and superior parietal lobe that were previously associated with executively demanding tasks.
source: Indeed, the upregulation of left SMG after cTBS of AG extended into the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and superior parietal lobe (SPL) that were previously associated with executively demanding tasks (Humphreys et al., 2015) and are part of a multi-domain control system (Duncan, 2010; Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of results with citations to previous work.

claim: The intraparietal sulcus and superior parietal lobe are part of a multi-domain control system.
source: Indeed, the upregulation of left SMG after cTBS of AG extended into the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and superior parietal lobe (SPL) that were previously associated with executively demanding tasks (Humphreys et al., 2015) and are part of a multi-domain control system (Duncan, 2010; Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: The strong perturbation effect on the phonological task after cTBS over SMG might be explained by the fact that (higher-level) semantic regions were not able to support task processing after disruption of the control network.
source: In contrast, the strong perturbation effect on the phonological task after cTBS over SMG might be explained by the fact that (higher-level) semantic regions were not able to support task processing after disruption of the control network.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: Both AG and aIFG were associated with executive control over semantic processing, although to a different degree.
source: With respect to the role of the observed regions in semantic processing, both AG and aIFG were associated with executive control over semantic processing, although to a different degree (Noonan et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: Left AG corresponds to a high-level cross-modal convergence zone for concept retrieval and the integration of meaning and event representations and provides access to semantics.
source: Left AG corresponds to a high-level cross-modal convergence zone for concept retrieval and the integration of meaning and event representations and provides access to semantics (Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: The ventral AG was associated with automatic semantic retrieval.
source: In particular, the ventral AG (overlapping with our stimulation site) was associated with automatic semantic retrieval, while a more dorsal subregion within the AG was assigned a role in controlled semantic retrieval (Noonan et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: A more dorsal subregion within the AG was assigned a role in controlled semantic retrieval.
source: In particular, the ventral AG (overlapping with our stimulation site) was associated with automatic semantic retrieval, while a more dorsal subregion within the AG was assigned a role in controlled semantic retrieval (Noonan et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: aIFG is an important node for top-down control during semantic processing and lexical retrieval.
source: aIFG, on the other hand, is an important node for top-down control during semantic processing and lexical retrieval (Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: Disruption of AG induced a functional disconnection by impairing the transfer of stimulus related activity from AG to aIFG.
source: Consequently, the observed network effect in our study might indicate that disruption of AG induced a functional disconnection by impairing the transfer of stimulus related activity from AG to aIFG, thereby necessitating the contribution of more domain-general resources under semantic conditions with increased task difficulty.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting mechanism of disruption.

claim: Most semantic tasks deactivate the core AG and rather activate neighbouring intraparietal sulcus.
source: A recent meta-analysis showed that most semantic tasks deactivate the core AG and rather activate neighbouring intraparietal sulcus (among other regions) (Humphreys et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous meta-analysis findings with citation.

claim: Left AG is clearly engaged by non-semantic domains such as memory and social cognition.
source: On the other hand, left AG is clearly engaged by non-semantic domains such as memory and social cognition (Bzdok et al., 2016; Humphreys et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: The semantic task might have particularly engaged semantic working memory processes that contributed to the observed positive AG activation.
source: In our study, the semantic task might have particularly engaged semantic working memory processes that contributed to the observed positive AG activation (Vigneau et al., 2006).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation.

claim: The effects of a focal perturbation are not restricted to the stimulated area itself but might rather affect a larger network.
source: First, they implicate that the effects of a focal perturbation are not restricted to the stimulated area itself but might rather affect a larger network (see Bestmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation.

claim: Remote effects may occur in distant cognitive network nodes.
source: Specifically, our data indicate that remote effects may occur in distant cognitive network nodes.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: Behavioural measures alone might not be sufficient to map a cTBS-induced perturbation effect.
source: Notably, the strong modulation of task-specific activity patterns in the absence of a significant disruption of the mean semantic response speed after AG cTBS indicates that behavioural measures alone might not be sufficient to map a cTBS-induced perturbation effect.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting limitations of behavioral measures.

claim: Some modulatory effects induced by non-invasive brain stimulation might only be captured on the neural network level and most likely originate from a modulation of the effective connectivity in a network.
source: Rather, some modulatory effects induced by non-invasive brain stimulation might only be captured on the neural network level and most likely originate from a modulation of the effective connectivity in a network.
evidence: Interpretation of results suggesting importance of network-level analysis.

claim: Without cTBS, there might be a weak facilitatory connectivity between AG and aIFG that turned into a strong inhibition after cTBS.
source: Indeed, our winning model revealed a positive intrinsic connection between AG and aIFG, indicating that without cTBS, there might be a (weak) facilitatory connectivity between both regions that turned into a strong inhibition after cTBS.
evidence: Interpretation of DCM results.

claim: The observed upregulation of a neighbouring parieto-frontal network for phonological processing might indicate some degree of degeneracy in the language network.
source: Secondly, the observed upregulation of a neighbouring parieto-frontal network for phonological processing might indicate some degree of degeneracy (Price and Friston, 2002) in the language network that might have partly enabled cross-modal compensation even after inhibition of a large part of the semantic network.
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation.

claim: cTBS may give rise to an acute adaptive reorganization within the non-targeted functional loops of another network to compensate for the cTBS-induced suppression of task-specific neuronal activity.
source: This is compatible with the notion that cTBS may give rise to an acute adaptive reorganization within the non-targeted functional loops of another network to compensate for the cTBS-induced suppression of task-specific neuronal activity (Hartwigsen and Siebner, 2012).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation.

claim: The observed greater resilience of the semantic relative to the phonological network against the behavioural lesion effect was underpinned by a difference in the flexible recruitment of neighbouring networks that was selectively observed for the semantic task.
source: The observed greater resilience of the semantic relative to the phonological network against the behavioural lesion effect was underpinned by a difference in the flexible recruitment of neighbouring networks that was selectively observed for the semantic task.
evidence: Interpretation of results comparing semantic and phonological networks.

claim: The difference in the flexible recruitment of neighbouring networks for semantic and phonological processes likely reflects the engagement of higher- vs. lower-level processes in both tasks.
source: The difference in the flexible recruitment of neighbouring networks for semantic and phonological processes likely reflects the engagement of higher- vs. lower-level processes in both tasks.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: The optimal DCM identified the SMG as the most likely source of the driving input among the selected regions.
source: Indeed, our optimal DCM identified the SMG as the most likely source of the driving input among the selected regions.
evidence: DCM model selection results.

claim: Left AG receives information from the neighbouring SMG, which is compatible with the role of the AG as a heteromodal integration area.
source: This indicates that left AG receives information from the neighbouring SMG, which is compatible with the above-discussed role of the AG as a heteromodal integration area (Seghier, 2013).
evidence: Interpretation of DCM results with citation.

claim: Disruption of the lower-level SMG region was not sufficient to significantly affect semantic task processing.
source: Interestingly, disruption of this lower-level region was not sufficient to significantly affect semantic task processing.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: Some previous imaging studies reported increased task-related activity of the right-hemispheric homologue after perturbation of a left-hemispheric key region for speech or language that was interpreted as adaptive short-term compensation.
source: Some of these studies (Binney and Ralph, 2015; Hartwigsen et al., 2013; Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016) reported increased task-related activity of the right-hemispheric homologue after perturbation of a left-hemispheric key region for speech or language that was interpreted as adaptive short-term compensation.
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citations.

claim: Perturbation of left IFG increased the activation of left pMTG during the processing of weak semantic associations.
source: Another study (Hallam et al., 2016) found that perturbation of left IFG increased the activation of left pMTG during the processing of weak semantic associations, demonstrating that compensation can also occur between different semantic nodes within the same left hemispheric network.
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: After cTBS over left ATL, the right ATL increased its intrinsic facilitatory influence on left ATL.
source: Moreover, Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016 showed that after cTBS over left ATL, the right ATL increased its intrinsic facilitatory influence on left ATL, indicating a flexible, bilateral organization of the semantic system with a strong degree of adaptive plasticity.
evidence: Statement about previous research findings with citation.

claim: When lowering the threshold, neural activity in right AG was also decreased after cTBS of left AG.
source: When lowering the threshold, neural activity in right AG was also decreased after cTBS of left AG, indicating a strong cTBS-induced inhibition in the semantic network.
evidence: Additional analysis at lower threshold showing bilateral effects.

claim: Left AG is a strategic core region for semantic processes.
source: This suggests that left AG is a strategic core region for semantic processes, a notion that is compatible with the key role of the AG in all aspects of semantic processing that require concept retrieval (Binder et al., 2009; Seghier, 2013), including efficient retrieval of semantic information (Davey et al., 2015).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citations to previous work.

claim: The flexible recruitment after disruption of a semantic key node may include regions within the same left-hemispheric network, as well as contralateral homologous regions or neighbouring regions from a different network.
source: Together, the previous findings and our results demonstrate the potential for a flexible recruitment after disruption of a semantic key node that may include regions within the same left-hemispheric network, as well as contralateral homologous regions or neighbouring regions from a different network.
evidence: Synthesis of current and previous findings.

claim: The exact recruitment may depend on the degree of the disruption and the specific task demands.

claim: The observed upregulation of SMG is more compatible with the notion of an adaptive contribution of ipsilateral regions after a lesion of a strategic left-hemispheric area.
source: Our findings are more compatible with the notion of an adaptive contribution of ipsilateral regions after a lesion of a strategic left-hemispheric area (Heiss and Thiel, 2006), rather than supporting the concept of maladaptive plasticity after a release from the inhibition of neighbouring regions.
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation.

claim: Previous studies on post-stroke aphasia suggest that the upregulation of ipsi- vs. contralateral regions after stroke might depend on the site, size and extent of the lesion.
source: Indeed, previous studies on post-stroke aphasia suggest that the upregulation of ipsi- vs. contralateral regions after stroke might depend on the site, size and extent of the lesion (Chrysikou and Hamilton, 2011).

claim: Models of language recovery proposed that for smaller lesions of critical left-hemispheric language nodes, neighbouring perilesional regions might be adaptively recruited to subserve language function while more severe impairments might stronger draw on recruitment of homotopic regions.
source: Models of language recovery proposed that for smaller lesions of critical left-hemispheric language nodes, neighbouring perilesional regions might be adaptively recruited to subserve language function while more severe impairments might stronger draw on recruitment of homotopic regions (Hamilton et al., 2011).

claim: Even a relatively focal perturbation can already inhibit neural activity in a large network.
source: Our results show that even a relatively focal perturbation can already inhibit neural activity in a large network.

claim: The recruitment of neighbouring areas seems to be related to a high level of adaptation (i.e., the absence of a strong behavioural effect).
source: In our case, the recruitment of neighbouring areas seems to be related to a high level of adaptation (i.e., the absence of a strong behavioural effect), indicating a general flexibility of brain networks in terms of distributed processing.

claim: Neighbouring networks might bear the inherent potential to partially support task processing after a strategic lesion of one key region.
source: This is of potential relevance for understanding language recovery after left hemisphere stroke, indicating that neighbouring networks might bear the inherent potential to partially support task processing after a strategic lesion of one key region.

source: Our results help to unravel neural mechanisms of perturbation effects, indicating that cTBS not only influences neural activity in the stimulated region but also in remote areas.

source: Although the observed effects were transient, they were sufficient to influence task-related activity, connectivity, and behaviour, as evidenced by the significant correlation between individual connectivity strength and delay in response speed.

claim: Combining TMS with effective connectivity analyses of fMRI data is valuable to map the neural consequences of a focal perturbation.
source: This demonstrates the value of combining TMS with effective connectivity analyses of fMRI data to map the neural consequences of a focal perturbation and might further inform models of language reorganization in post-stroke aphasia.
